artworks.title: Artemis and Hyperion
artworks.description: Watts' Symbolist canvas pairs Artemis with Hyperion, the Titan of light whose name still means 'the High One.' The painting treats the Hesiodic father of Helios, Selene and Eos as a luminous presence rather than a mere genealogy — Hyperion as living light beside the huntress.

artworks.title: A Study for Hyperion
artworks.description: A preparatory study held at Somerville College, Oxford, for Watts' Hyperion imagery. The Titan of watchful light is reduced to a concentrated figure study — Victorian idealism reaching for the Hesiodic sun before the Olympian Helios took the chariot.

artworks.title: The Fall of the Titans
artworks.description: Haarlem Mannerism's showpiece in Copenhagen hurls Hyperion's generation into Tartarus — the Titans cast down after Zeus' victory. Hyperion, father of the lights of heaven, falls with his brothers in a writhing mass of foreshortened nudes.

artworks.title: The Fall of the Titans
artworks.description: A Rubensian Fall of the Titans in Brussels restages the Titanomachy's end: the elder gods of light and sky plunge as Olympus rises. Hyperion belongs to that defeated generation — the High One cast from the upper air his children would later rule.

popCulture.title: Hyperion (moon)
popCulture.description: Saturn's chaotic tumbling moon took the Titan of light's name — Hyperion as a sponge-shaped world at the edge of the rings.

popCulture.title: Hyperion (Titan)
popCulture.description: The High One who fathered Helios, Selene and Eos remains the poetic name for towering light — Hyperion as sun before the Olympian sun.
